lead: Every digital system needs a rule for when a signal is valid. A synchronous system clocks every register from one clock. Parts that share a frequency but not a phase are mesochronous, parts with nearly equal frequencies are plesiochronous, and parts with no clock at all are asynchronous or self-timed. This chapter classifies these schemes, shows how clock skew and jitter eat into a synchronous design's clock period, and builds the self-timed alternative from handshakes, completion detection and the Muller C-element.
prereq: You need: setup, hold and clock-to-Q from Chapter 4.6, and pipelines from Chapter 4.7.

blocks.text: Each class needs its own interface. Mesochronous parts need a phase adjustment, such as a variable delay line or a small FIFO. Plesiochronous parts need an elastic buffer that now and then repeats or drops a word as the clocks slip. A truly asynchronous input reaching a clocked system needs a synchronizer, usually two flip-flops in series, so that a metastable first flip-flop has a whole period to settle before anyone reads it.

sections.h3: Synchronous design: clock skew and jitter

blocks.text: Clock skew δ is the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at two registers: δ = arrival at the capturing register − arrival at the launching register. It is spatial and constant from cycle to cycle, caused by different wire lengths, loads and buffers in the clock tree. Clock jitter t<sub>jit</sub> is the variation of one register's edge from cycle to cycle around its ideal time, caused by supply noise and the clock generator. For the worst case, the launch edge may come t<sub>jit</sub> late and the capture edge t<sub>jit</sub> early:
Here the setup check: T is the clock period and t<sub>logic</sub> the longest logic delay. Positive δ (clock travelling with the data) gives the data extra time.

Here the hold check: t<sub>cq,cd</sub> and t<sub>logic,cd</sub> are the contamination (fastest) delays of the register and the shortest logic path. Positive δ lets the capture register look later, so new data can arrive before its hold time ends.

So positive skew helps setup and hurts hold; negative skew (clock against the data) helps hold and costs speed; jitter only hurts. Designers keep both small with balanced clock distribution: an H-tree, whose equal-length branches reach every leaf at the same time, or a clock grid that shorts the tree's ends together, with buffers along the way and a phase-locked or delay-locked loop to line the on-chip clock up with the outside one.

A self-timed circuit replaces the global clock with local handshakes. A stage tells the next that its output is valid with a request (Req), and the receiver answers that it has taken the data with an acknowledge (Ack). The four-phase, or return-to-zero, protocol has four events per transfer: Req↑ (data valid), Ack↑ (data taken), Req↓, Ack↓ (ready for the next one). The two-phase protocol uses every transition as an event, one Req edge and one Ack edge per transfer: faster, but the logic must respond to edges rather than levels.

The receiver must know when the logic has finished. Dual-rail coding sends each bit on two wires (t, f): (0, 0) is a spacer meaning not yet valid, (1, 0) means 1, (0, 1) means 0, and (1, 1) is never used. A bit is complete when t + f = 1, and the word is complete when every bit is. DCVSL produces both rails naturally, which is why self-timed adders often use it. The cheaper bundled-data method keeps single-rail data and sends Req through a matched delay line slightly slower than the logic's worst case.

The Muller C-element joins handshakes. Its output goes to 1 when both inputs are 1, goes to 0 when both are 0, and otherwise holds its value. In CMOS it is two series pMOS and two series nMOS driving a node held by a weak keeper inverter. One C-element per stage, driven by the stage's incoming Req and the inverted output of the next stage's C-element, forms a Muller pipeline: the self-timed version of Chapter 4.7.

Self-timed design removes clock power and clock skew, runs at the average delay of the data rather than the worst case, and tolerates supply and process variation. Its costs are extra wires (dual rail doubles them), completion-detection area, hazard-free logic design and weaker tool support, so most chips are synchronous with self-timed islands in memories, FIFOs and interfaces.

examples.question: A register-to-register path has t<sub>cq</sub> = 0.25 ns, t<sub>logic</sub> = 1.8 ns (longest), t<sub>su</sub> = 0.10 ns, t<sub>h</sub> = 0.08 ns, contamination delays t<sub>cq,cd</sub> = 0.15 ns and t<sub>logic,cd</sub> = 0.20 ns, and jitter t<sub>jit</sub> = 0.05 ns. Find the shortest clock period and check hold for skew (a) δ = 0, (b) δ = +0.2 ns, (c) δ = −0.2 ns. Fix any hold failure.
steps: Fixed sums: t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>logic</sub> + t<sub>su</sub> + 2t<sub>jit</sub> = 0.25 + 1.8 + 0.10 + 0.10 = 2.25 ns. Short path: t<sub>cq,cd</sub> + t<sub>logic,cd</sub> = 0.15 + 0.20 = 0.35 ns.
(a) δ = 0: T ≥ 2.25 ns, f<sub>max</sub> = 1 ÷ 2.25 ns = 444.4 MHz. Hold needs 0.35 ≥ 0.08 + 0 + 0.10 = 0.18 ns: passes with 0.17 ns to spare.
Fix for (b): add a buffer of at least 0.03 ns to the short path only (for example 0.05 ns): 0.35 + 0.05 = 0.40 ≥ 0.38 ns. The long path, and so f<sub>max</sub>, is unchanged.
(c) δ = −0.2 ns: T ≥ 2.25 + 0.2 = 2.45 ns, f<sub>max</sub> = 408.2 MHz. Hold needs 0.35 ≥ 0.08 − 0.2 + 0.10 = −0.02 ns: passes with 0.37 ns to spare.
examples.answer: δ = 0: 2.25 ns (444.4 MHz), hold passes. δ = +0.2 ns: 2.05 ns (487.8 MHz) but hold fails by 0.03 ns until a 0.05 ns buffer is added to the short path. δ = −0.2 ns: 2.45 ns (408.2 MHz), hold passes easily.

examples.question: A Muller C-element starts with inputs A = B = 0 and output Z = 0. The inputs then change as (A, B) = (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1). Give Z after each change.
steps: Rule: Z becomes 1 only when A = B = 1, becomes 0 only when A = B = 0, and holds otherwise.
(0, 1): inputs differ, Z holds 1. An AND gate would already have fallen to 0 here; this memory is what makes the C-element a sequential circuit.
examples.answer: Z = 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1 after the six changes: the output moves only when both inputs agree, which is how a C-element waits for two handshakes.

traps: Sign of skew. With δ = capture arrival − launch arrival, positive δ relaxes setup (T + δ) and tightens hold (t<sub>h</sub> + δ). State the definition before writing either check.
Treating jitter like skew. Skew is constant and can help one check; jitter varies from cycle to cycle, appears as 2t<sub>jit</sub> and never helps.
Fixing a hold failure by slowing the clock. T is not in the hold check; add delay to the short path or reduce the skew.
Calling plesiochronous clocks mesochronous. Mesochronous means the same frequency with a fixed phase offset; plesiochronous frequencies differ slightly, so the phase keeps drifting.
Drawing a C-element as an AND gate. It holds its output while the inputs disagree; an AND gate does not.

quiz.q: Name the four timing classes of digital systems.
How do clock skew and clock jitter differ?
quiz.a: Skew is a fixed, spatial difference in when the same edge reaches two registers. Jitter is a temporal, cycle-to-cycle variation of one edge around its ideal time. Skew can help setup or hold; jitter only reduces the margin.

quiz.q: Why does dual-rail coding need a spacer state?
quiz.a: The receiver detects completion when every bit pair has exactly one rail high. Returning all rails to (0, 0) between words makes every new word a fresh 0-to-1 transition, so a stale value cannot be mistaken for a new one.

quiz.q: A path has t<sub>cq</sub> = 0.2 ns, t<sub>logic</sub> = 1.5 ns, t<sub>su</sub> = 0.1 ns, t<sub>jit</sub> = 0.02 ns and skew δ = −0.15 ns. Find the shortest clock period and f<sub>max</sub>.
Why does positive skew help setup but hurt hold?
quiz.a: Positive δ means the capture register sees the edge later. For setup, the data launched at the earlier edge gets δ more time, so T + δ appears on the left. For hold, the capture register keeps sampling until later, so new data from the same edge must not arrive before t<sub>h</sub> + δ, a harder target.

quiz.q: When is a self-timed design a better choice than a synchronous one?
quiz.a: When the average delay is much shorter than the worst case (it runs at data speed), when clock power or clock distribution is a problem, or when blocks with unrelated timing must be joined. It costs extra wires, completion logic and harder testing, so it suits FIFOs, interfaces and low-power islands rather than a whole chip.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large chips are globally asynchronous, locally synchronous (GALS): clocked islands joined by asynchronous FIFOs, with clock-domain-crossing checks in every sign-off flow. Search next for "GALS" and "clock domain crossing".
